newsitem.title: USA: Narrower US March trade gap sign of robust economy.
newsitem.headline: Narrower US March trade gap sign of robust economy.

text.p: Exports surged for a second consecutive month in March, shrinking the U.S. international trade gap by a whopping 19.3 percent and underscoring the ongoing strength of the U.S. economy, analysts said.
The Commerce Department reported on Wednesday that the March trade deficit shrunk to $8.51 billion from an upwardly revised $10.54 billion in February, largely due to a 4.1 percent jump in exports.
Aircraft and gold exports each jumped by over $700 million in the month, fuelling the overall gain in that sector.
Wall Street economists, skeptical of whether exports could match the substantial 4.0 percent improvement seen in February, had expected the gap to shrink slightly to $10.3 billion.

"When you have record exports and the dollar was at such a strong level that tells you something about the U.S. economy," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at REFCO Group Ltd in Chicago.
During March the dollar was surging to its highest level against the yen in over four years, and to near three-year peaks against the mark.

Economists said the export strength in the March trade report would necessitate slight upward revisions to first quarter U.S. gross domestic product growth, which came in at a preliminary 5.6 percent -- the fastest pace in more than nine years.
Along with the strong export growth the report showed that imports rose 1.2 percent in March to $84.99 billion from an upwardly revised $84.01 billion.
The touchy deficit with China shrank by 22.4 percent to $2.59 billion in March, while the politically sensitive shortfall with Japan rose 8.3 percent to $4.61 billion.
"There is typically an improvement with China in March so I wouldn't read too much into that," said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc-CRT.
"But it looks like the balance with the newly industrializing countries in Asia improved significantly and lower oil import prices led to another very good balance with OPEC."
The Commerce Department reported that the price of imported crude oil fell to an average $18.72 per barrel in March from $20.49 per barrel in February.
But the strong export numbers garnered the most attention, encouraging currency traders to push the dollar substantially higher in the report's aftermath.

"It's good news for the dollar," said Gary Thayer, senior economist, A.G. Edwards & Sons. "There have been a couple of reports lately, particularly the Japanese trade surplus widening, which had people concerned that our trade deficit would also widen."
Manufacturing and advanced technology exports led the way, with agricultural exports dropping off slightly and crude oil exports also falling.
Overall exports totalled a record $76.48 billion in the month of March.

"The last couple of export numbers combined with recent (purchasing managers) surveys suggest that the level for the first quarter and starting level for the second quarter looks very healthy," said NationsBanc's Rothfield.
